label: Divrei HaYamim Aleph (1 Chronicles) — Part 2 — Chapters 10–29
summary_plain: Divrei HaYamim Aleph chapters 10 through 29 retell Dawid's reign from the death of Sha'ul to Dawid's final charge to Shelomoh. Dawid captures Yerushalayim and brings the Ark of the Covenant into the city with singing and dancing. He desires to build a house for YHWH, but YHWH says: Your son will build the house — I will establish his throne forever. Dawid prepares the materials for the temple, organizes the Levitical musicians and gatekeepers, and charges Shelomoh: Be strong and courageous. Know the Creator of your father and serve him with a whole heart.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from DSS fragments (4QChr) and the Orit Ge'ez. The Chronicler retells Dawid's reign with a distinctive emphasis: the military and political failures recorded in Shemu'el (Bat-Sheva, Amnon, Avshalom's revolt) are largely omitted. The Chronicler focuses on Dawid's role as temple preparer, worship organizer, and covenant transmitter. This is not historical falsification — it is theological selection. The Chronicler writes for the post-exilic community that needs to know its liturgical and institutional origins. Dawid's organization of the Levitical musicians (chapters 25-26) establishes the worship infrastructure that produced the Tehillim. The Chronicler's Dawid is the singer, the worshipper, the one who prepared everything so that YHWH's house could be built. The covenant promise in chapter 17 parallels 2 Shemu'el 7 — YHWH's unconditional oath to Dawid's line.

key_terms.definition: The Chronicler's presentation of Dawid focuses almost entirely on Temple preparation and covenant worship. The failures recorded in Shemu'el — Bat-Sheva, Uriyah, the rape of Tamar, Avshalom's rebellion — are absent. This is not falsification; it is a different lens. The Chronicler presents the ideal Dawid: the king who organized the Levites, instituted music, prepared materials for the Temple, and transmitted the covenant to Shelomoh.

1 Divrei HaYamim 13-16: Dawid attempts to bring the Ark to Yerushalayim. The first attempt fails when Uzza touches the Ark and dies — the Ark had not been carried by Levites as the Torah required. After three months at the house of Oved-Edom (who was blessed), Dawid brings the Ark properly with the Levites carrying it. Dawid dances before YHWH with all his strength.

1 Divrei HaYamim 17: YHWH's covenant with Dawid — 'I will establish him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be established forever.' The Chronicler records the Davidic covenant as the foundational promise that undergirds the entire Temple project: the Temple is built in the context of an eternal covenant with the Davidic line.

1 Divrei HaYamim 28-29: Dawid assembles all the leaders of Yisra'el and charges Shelomoh publicly to build the Temple. 'Be strong and courageous and do it. Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for YHWH the Creator is with you. He will not leave you or forsake you.' Dawid then gives Shelomoh the full architectural plan for the Temple, received from YHWH.

1 Divrei HaYamim 25: Dawid organized 288 musicians from the Levites — from the families of Asaf, Heman, and Yedutun — into 24 divisions who served in rotation. This is the first systematic organization of covenant worship music. Dawid is both organizer and psalmist: the same king who organized the music also wrote much of what was sung.

1 Divrei HaYamim 29:10-19: Dawid's prayer at the assembly where the people bring offerings for the Temple is a comprehensive confession of YHWH's sovereignty. 'Yours, O YHWH, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty, for all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours.' He acknowledges that even the wealth they are giving belongs to YHWH: 'all things come from you, and of your own have we given you.'

key_terms.term: The Temple Plan Given by Ruach
key_terms.definition: 1 Divrei HaYamim 28:11-19: Dawid gives Shelomoh the detailed Temple plan — not invented by Dawid but received from YHWH. 'All this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of YHWH, all the work to be done according to the plan.' The Temple is not a human architectural project; it is YHWH's own design given through covenant communication.

1 Divrei HaYamim 16: when the Ark is installed in the tent Dawid has prepared, he appoints Levites to minister before the Ark, to invoke YHWH, to give thanks, and to sing praises. The psalm composed for the occasion is a composite of Tehillim 105, 96, and 106 — giving thanks, declaring YHWH's deeds among the nations, and declaring 'his steadfast love endures forever.'

1 Divrei HaYamim 21: Dawid's census brings a plague. The plague-angel stops at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Dawid buys the site and builds an altar. 'I will not take for YHWH what is yours, nor offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing.' This site becomes the Temple Mount — the same location as Avraham's binding of Yitzhaq on Mount Moriyah.

1 Divrei HaYamim 17:1: 'Now when Dawid lived in his house, Dawid said to Natan the prophet, Behold, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of the covenant of YHWH is under a tent.' Dawid's desire to build a Temple is genuine — he is troubled that YHWH's Ark is in a tent while he lives in a cedar palace. YHWH's response (the Davidic covenant) affirms the desire but transfers the building to Shelomoh.

faq.question: Why does the Chronicler omit Dawid's failures that are recorded in Shemu'el?
faq.answer: The Chronicler is not writing a comprehensive biography of Dawid — that work is in Shemu'el and Melakhim. The Chronicler is writing a theological history focused on the Temple and the Davidic covenant. His purpose is to show the community returning from exile what the ideal covenant king looked like in relation to the Temple and worship. The Bat-Sheva affair, the Avshalom rebellion, the census (which is included, because it explains the Temple site) — these are not suppressed; they are present in the Torah itself. The Chronicler chooses to emphasize what the covenant community needs to understand: how Dawid organized worship, prepared materials, and transmitted the covenant to Shelomoh.

faq.question: What does Dawid's charge to Shelomoh reveal about covenant transmission?
faq.answer: Dawid's charge in 1 Divrei HaYamim 28 is both a command and a covenant act. He assembles all the leaders of Yisra'el as witnesses. He delivers the covenant instruction publicly: know YHWH with a whole heart, serve him with a willing mind, be strong and courageous. He gives Shelomoh the written architectural plan. He prays publicly for Shelomoh's heart to be covenant-faithful. The charge is the act of covenant transmission from one generation to the next — the same structure as Moshe's charge to Yehoshua before the conquest. The covenant king's death includes the deliberate passing of covenant responsibility to the next generation.

faq.question: What does Dawid's final prayer reveal about covenant stewardship?
faq.answer: The prayer in chapter 29 is theologically decisive. After the people bring massive offerings for the Temple, Dawid prays: 'All things come from you, and of your own have we given you.' This declaration strips the gift of any claim to human merit. The wealth is YHWH's wealth, returned to him. The Temple is YHWH's project, carried out with YHWH's resources. Dawid then prays for Shelomoh's heart to be covenant-faithful. The prayer holds the community's greatest act of generosity in its proper place: not as an achievement that earns YHWH's favor, but as an act of returning what already belongs to him.

faq.question: What does the failed Ark transport teach about covenant worship?
faq.answer: The first attempt to bring the Ark used a cart — the same method the Plishtim had used to return it. This was practical but covenant-wrong. The Torah specified that Levites were to carry the Ark on poles inserted through the rings (Shemot 25). Uzza's death when he touched the Ark to steady it was not a punishment for good intentions — it was the consequence of handling a covenant object incorrectly. YHWH's covenant instructions about the Ark were not bureaucratic formality; they were the form by which the covenant community expressed its understanding of YHWH's holiness. Getting the form right is not legalism — it is the community's embodied acknowledgment that YHWH is not like other objects.

faq.question: What is the theological significance of Dawid being a man of war in relation to the Temple?
faq.answer: YHWH explicitly tells Dawid through Natan that Dawid cannot build the Temple because he is a man of war and has shed much blood (1 Divrei HaYamim 22:8). The Temple is a house of peace (shalom), and its builder must be a man of peace. Shelomoh's name means peace. The Temple project requires a different covenant posture than the military campaigns that established the kingdom's security. Dawid's role is to prepare — to gather materials, establish the workforce, organize the Levites, purchase the site, and transmit the plan. Shelomoh's role is to build. YHWH assigns different covenant roles to different covenant servants based on what each is equipped to do.

faq.question: What does the Levitical music organization reveal about covenant worship?
faq.answer: Dawid's organization of 288 Levitical musicians into 24 rotating divisions is not incidental. The covenant community's worship is not improvised — it is organized, trained, and structured. The Levites who sang before YHWH were 'trained in singing to YHWH, all who were skillful.' Skill in worship is a covenant requirement, not an aesthetic preference. The 24 divisions rotating service means that trained covenant worship is maintained continuously — not dependent on any one person's availability or inspiration. Dawid understood that YHWH's worship required the community's best and most organized effort, not whatever was convenient.

faq.question: What does the threshing floor purchase establish for the Temple site?
faq.answer: The threshing floor of Ornan (Araunah in Shemu'el) was purchased by Dawid at full price — 600 gold shekels in Divrei HaYamim. The site is Mount Moriyah, identified in 2 Divrei HaYamim 3:1 as the place where YHWH appeared to Dawid and where Avraham bound Yitzhaq. The purchase establishes legal, covenant ownership of the site. The Temple is built on ground that YHWH designated, that the plague-angel marked, that the first covenant patriarch sanctified, and that the covenant king bought. The site's covenant history runs from Avraham through Dawid to Shelomoh's Temple.

faq.question: What does the Temple plan 'given by YHWH in writing' signify?
faq.answer: The Temple's architectural plan was given to Dawid by YHWH — 'all this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of YHWH.' The Temple is not a human design. It is YHWH's own design for his covenant dwelling. This matters for how the Temple is understood: it is not a monument to Dawid's glory or a demonstration of Shelomoh's wisdom. It is a structure built to YHWH's specification, for YHWH's purpose. The same covenant logic that required the Mishkan to be built exactly according to the heavenly pattern (Shemot 25:9) applies to the permanent Temple. The form is YHWH's; the community builds it according to that form.

faq.question: What lesson did David learn from the failed first attempt to bring the Ark?
faq.answer: In 1 Divrei HaYamim 13, David moved the Ark on a new cart — following a Philistine method, not the Torah's instruction. When Uzza reached out and touched the Ark, YHWH struck him dead. David was angry and afraid and left the Ark at Obed-Edom's house for three months. When David tried again in chapter 15, he said: 'No one but the Levites may carry the ark of YHWH, for YHWH chose them to carry the ark of YHWH and to minister to him forever.' The lesson is explicit and covenant-specific: how YHWH is served matters, not only the intention behind the service. The Philistines who returned the Ark on a cart were not covenant keepers; Yisra'el is held to the covenant standard. Good intentions are not sufficient when YHWH has specified the method. The Levites carry the Ark; that is not negotiable by inventive improvisation, however well-meant.

faq.question: What does 1 Divrei HaYamim 28-29 reveal about the Temple plan?
faq.answer: David's final address in 1 Divrei HaYamim 28-29 reveals that the Temple plan came directly from YHWH: 'All this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of YHWH, all the work to be done according to the plan.' The Temple is not David's architectural vision — it is YHWH's blueprint delivered to David. This parallels the Mishkan (Tabernacle) that Moshe built according to the heavenly pattern shown on the mountain. YHWH's dwelling in the community's midst follows YHWH's own design, not human creativity. David's wealth prepared for the Temple is recorded in extraordinary detail — gold by weight for every golden vessel, silver by weight for every silver vessel, bronze, iron, wood, onyx, gem settings. The community responds by giving willingly and joyfully. David's prayer closes the moment: 'Who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you.'
